rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi pictures date palms and grapes as the principal orchard produce, with patches for grains and seasonal fruits also covered by the verse’s many fruits and eating.
rows.anchor: The words “many fruits” and “from which you also eat” are actually pointing to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He identifies the unnamed tree as the olive, whose production on Mount Sinai was famous; its food product was prized among Arabs and regarded as edible and religiously significant by the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: refers to an olive tree. Though it is not named, the traits mentioned clearly point to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi glosses ṣibgh as curry and describes the olive product as a tasty, butterlike curry that gives vitality to those who eat it.
rows.anchor: means “curry.” It was also like a tasty curry like butter that would provide vitality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for curry is left indefinite to express the product’s grandeur.
rows.anchor: It is mentioned in an undefined way to express its grandeur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains ʿibrah as crossing from a perceptible reality to a lesson; the cattle too offer a great lesson when people reflect.
rows.anchor: to cross over from reality to another and learn a lesson from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite noun ʿibrah magnifies the lesson carried by the signs just mentioned, especially the cattle.
rows.anchor: It is used as an undefined noun to magnify it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second object of nusqikum is omitted; 16:66 supplies the pure milk wording. Filling the ellipses yields the sense that God gives pure milk from within animals, amidst faeces and blood.
rows.anchor: If all these suppressions are taken into account, the overall meaning would be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond milk and food, cattle provide transport and labor, help harvest crops, and supply meat, hides, wool, and manure; some animals are useful chiefly as food.
rows.anchor: They are used to travel and as beasts of burden. They help people in harvesting crops.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi introduces the instructions in 24:27–34 as something to read against the preceding background of practices that produce social unity.
rows.anchor: unity are produced in the society.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi takes istiʾnās here to mean introducing oneself before entering another person’s home.
rows.anchor: means “to be introduced.” The word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Buyūt means residential houses where a person’s family lives, as clarified by the following verse.
rows.anchor: residential houses – as explained in the next verse – where a person’s family lives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Visitors must not barge into others’ homes: they should introduce themselves with salām at the door, enter only after a response and permission, and otherwise return.
rows.anchor: If they receive a response and are granted permission, only then they should enter the house, otherwise they should return.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salām is a gracious way both to introduce oneself and to seek permission to enter.
rows.anchor: Saying salām is a very gracious way to introduce one’s self and to seek permission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greeting lets residents know who is visiting and why, so they can judge whether entry is suitable and whether the timing is appropriate.
rows.anchor: through this greeting the residents will come to know of the identity of the person and his purpose of coming

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking leave before entering was customary among civilized peoples and pre-Islamic Arab nobility; Islahi says Islam directed people to use salām for this purpose instead of adopting their wording.
rows.anchor: Amongst the nobility of the Arab jāhiliyyah this tradition also existed; in fact, the words that were used for this had almost the same meaning

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet taught visitors to say salām at the front door, repeat it three times if there is no answer, and then leave.
rows.anchor: The way taught by the Prophet (sws) to do this was that a person should say this word at the front door

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restriction prevents an unsuitable visitor from reaching the part of the home where women reside at an inappropriate time; only relatives of the household head or people he fully trusts may enter.
rows.anchor: only those people could enter the house who were either related to the head of the family or were fully trusted by him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder explains why the restriction is beneficial rather than burdensome: visitors are entering someone’s privacy and must observe decorum, while residents also benefit by observing the visit’s limits.
rows.anchor: this word is like a blessed reminder to the person who is visiting that he is intruding into the privacy of someone where he must follow certain decorum.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If permission-seeking shows no one is home to grant permission, a visitor must not enter unless permission is granted; if asked to leave, the visitor must return.
rows.anchor: The verse implies that if after seeking permission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although refusal may hurt, accepting it is the moral course: visitors cannot know residents’ circumstances and should value their convenience over personal ego, avoiding Satan’s guiles.
rows.anchor: One cannot know the circumstances of this refusal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated reminders of God’s knowledge address the inner evasions people may devise; commands alone cannot close these gaps, while awareness that God is always watching protects against Satan’s hidden ploys.
rows.anchor: God has knowledge of what you reveal and what you conceal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception concerns non-residential places used for some need or benefit, such as shops, travel lodges, hotels, and male meeting places; these may be entered without seeking permission.
rows.anchor: places of general need like shops, travel lodges and hotels etc. are examples of such places.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning about what God knows discourages people from exploiting the exception, such as entering a women’s area and claiming to have mistaken it for the men’s area.
rows.anchor: he puts forth the excuse that he thought this was the male compound.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restraining the gaze and guarding private parts are requisites of faith.
rows.anchor: restraining the eyes and guarding the private parts is a requisite of faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The min in “lower part of their gaze” calls for restraining the gaze enough to prevent undue liberty with women in the household, the context the directive addresses.
rows.anchor: the purpose is to lower the gaze to the extent that they do not take undue liberty regarding the women of the house

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permission to enter a home where women are present is a relief for relatives and people trusted by the household head, especially since homes then and now may lack a separate men’s reception area.
rows.anchor: only to provide relief regarding the relatives and people of trust of the head of the house.
